clue.text: Pirate's brother William is a hedge-cutter

parts.note: Bill is the usual short form of the name William
Captain Hook is the pirate of Peter Pan, so the pirate gives his surname

explanation.surface: A family note: the buccaneer's brother Will makes his living trimming hedges.
explanation.walkthrough: The pirate is Captain Hook of Peter Pan, so his brother William would be Bill Hook; the charade puts BILL before HOOK.
explanation.definitionFit: A billhook is a curved-bladed chopping tool used for laying and trimming hedges.

clue.text: It houses a French girl in part of East London

definitions.text: It houses a French girl in part of East London

indicators.note: the French article and the girl are placed inside the district's name

parts.note: Bow is a district in the East End of London
un is the French for a
gal is an informal word for a girl

explanation.surface: A single-storey house in Bow is home to a young French woman.
explanation.walkthrough: BOW is an East London district; UN (French for 'a') and GAL (girl) go inside it. The whole clue also describes the answer: a dwelling that houses the French girl.
explanation.definitionFit: A bungalow is a single-storey dwelling, the kind of home that could lodge a lodger in Bow.

clue.text: What circulation is to a newspaper

definitions.text: What circulation is to a newspaper

parts.words: What circulation is to a newspaper
parts.note: circulation, the number of copies sold, is what keeps a paper alive, just as the circulation of blood keeps a body alive

explanation.surface: A media observation on how vital sales figures are to a paper.
explanation.walkthrough: Circulation has two senses: copies sold, and blood moving round the body. The answer is the vital fluid, used figuratively for whatever keeps something going.
explanation.definitionFit: Something essential to survival is called its life-blood, as blood circulating is to a body.

clue.text: Hyperion,.. for instance, looked right in socks

indicators.note: the abbreviation for right is put inside the word for socks

parts.note: hose is an old word for stockings or socks

explanation.surface: The Titan Hyperion cuts a fine figure wearing his socks.
explanation.walkthrough: Hyperion was a famous British racehorse, winner of the 1933 Derby; 'for instance' marks it as an example. 'looked' only joins the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Hyperion was a celebrated Derby-winning racehorse, an example of a thoroughbred steed.

clue.text: Love ? Less about love-it's spelling disaster

parts.note: love is zero in tennis scoring, written as O

indicators.note: the word for less goes round the second love, so it surrounds it

parts.note: minus means less, as in five minus two
love is zero in tennis, written as O

explanation.surface: A lovelorn lament that losing love spells calamity.
explanation.walkthrough: Both loves are O, the tennis zero; 'about' puts MINUS round the second to give MINOUS after the first O. 'spelling' means portending, not writing.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ominous foretells calamity, as dark clouds portend a storm.

clue.text: Supporter of something laid on the table

definitions.text: Supporter of something laid on the table

parts.words: Supporter of something laid on the table
parts.note: the thing laid is an egg, by a hen, and the supporter is a small cup holding it at breakfast

explanation.surface: Someone backs a proposal laid on the table at a meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Laid on the table' suggests a motion put before a committee; here it is an egg (something laid) served on the breakfast table, and its holder.
explanation.definitionFit: An egg-cup is a small cup that holds a boiled egg upright at the breakfast table.

clue.text: Vexatious being without work when going the: pace.

indicators.note: being without here means being on the outside of, so the vexing word surrounds the work

parts.note: galling means irritating or vexatious
op is short for opus, a work of music

explanation.surface: Something annoying happens when you're out of a job and racing along.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is the old sense 'outside': GALLING wraps round OP, short for opus.
explanation.definitionFit: Galloping means moving at full speed, as a horse at its fastest gait.

clue.text: Against having a shot in the river

parts.note: con means against, as in pros and cons
a go is an attempt or shot, as in have a go

explanation.surface: Someone opposed to taking a try at the river crossing.
explanation.definitionFit: The Congo is the great river of central Africa.

clue.text: No chop and change in this S American style

indicators.note: change tells us the letters of these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A fashion tip: don't cut it, just swap to this South American look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' rearranges NOCHOP to give the cloak's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A poncho is a blanket-like cloak with a head opening, a traditional garment of South America.

clue.text: How to hole a golf-ball uphill ? Skip-it!

indicators.note: in a down clue going uphill means reading from the bottom up, so the letters are turned round

parts.note: you putt the ball into the hole on a golf green
taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice on sinking an uphill putt, then telling someone to forget it.
explanation.walkthrough: PUTT IT (how to hole the ball) read upward in this down light gives the answer. 'Skip' is the definition, a verb meaning to prance.
explanation.definitionFit: To tittup is to move with a jaunty, prancing step, much as one might skip.

clue.text: One bird, about low marshy ground, brought back for the queen

indicators.note: brought back says the whole string of pieces is read in reverse order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
a tit is a small songbird
re means about or concerning
a fen is low-lying marshy land, as in the Fens of eastern England

explanation.surface: A single bird is fetched back from the marshes as a gift for the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: I, TIT, RE and FEN run together as ITITREFEN; 'brought back' turns the whole string round.
explanation.definitionFit: Nefertiti was the Egyptian royal consort of Akhenaten, famed for her painted bust.

clue.text: Material for Gilpin, taking direction north

parts.note: a line is a direction or course, as in line of march

explanation.surface: Gilpin is supplied with cloth, heading off northwards.
explanation.walkthrough: John Gilpin, of William Cowper's comic poem, was a 'linen-draper bold', so his material is this fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Linen is cloth woven from flax, the stock of Cowper's draper hero.

clue.text: A thousand dollars lost from speculation ? Go easy

indicators.note: lost from says the grand is taken away from the word for speculation

parts.note: a gamble is a speculation or risky venture
a grand, a thousand dollars, is abbreviated G

explanation.surface: After losing a thousand bucks on a risky bet, the advice is to take it easy.
explanation.walkthrough: G is slang for a grand, a thousand dollars; 'lost from' removes it from GAMBLE.
explanation.definitionFit: To amble is to walk at a slow, relaxed pace.

clue.text: Conqueror of Italy to go short perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the words could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: An Italian conquest, which may have fallen short of its aims.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges TOGOSHORT.
explanation.definitionFit: The East Germanic tribe under Theodoric seized Italy in the late fifth century.

clue.text: Like. Dogberry's comparisons

parts.note: the constable Dogberry in Much Ado About Nothing garbles the saying that comparisons are odious, using a word meaning smelly

explanation.surface: A literary query about what Shakespeare's constable likens things to.
explanation.walkthrough: Dogberry, the bumbling constable of Much Ado About Nothing, says 'comparisons are odorous' when he means 'odious'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's malapropism swaps odious for a word meaning smelly, so his comparisons carry a scent.

clue.text: Man in charge of circus tent. employs cephalopods

parts.note: OC is Officer Commanding, the officer in charge of a unit
the big top is the main tent of a circus
uses means employs

explanation.surface: The ringmaster of the big top hires squid and their kin.
explanation.walkthrough: OC is the military Officer Commanding; TOP is from 'big top', the circus tent.
explanation.definitionFit: Octopuses are eight-armed molluscs of the class Cephalopoda, alongside squid and cuttlefish.

clue.text: Miss Laetitia's optical devices

definitions.meaning: Miss Laetitia Prism is the governess in Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest, so this is her surname with an S
glass blocks that split or bend light

explanation.surface: A lady's spectacles and lenses.
explanation.walkthrough: Laetitia is the first name of Miss Prism in Oscar Wilde's play; drop the apostrophe from her possessive surname.
explanation.definitionFit: The Wilde governess's surname with an S, and also triangular glass blocks that refract light.

clue.text: Play-time device

parts.note: not a toy for playtime but an instrument that keeps time while music is played

explanation.walkthrough: 'Play-time' suggests a school break; read it as keeping time while playing music.
explanation.definitionFit: A metronome ticks out a steady beat to keep a musician in tempo.

clue.text: Supporter has head broken and torn

indicators.note: broken says the letters of the word before it are rearranged

parts.note: rent means torn, as in a rent garment

explanation.surface: A fan suffers a broken head and ripped clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' rearranges HEAD to give ADHE; RENT, from 'torn', follows.
explanation.definitionFit: An adherent is a follower or devotee of a cause.

clue.text: Rode back, bringing it in to the news boss

indicators.note: in says the small word is placed inside the turned word
back says the word rode is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone rode back to deliver it to the head of the newsroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns RODE into EDOR, and 'in' puts IT inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An editor is the person in charge of a newspaper's content.

clue.text: Jury's recommendation about a bomb-dropper.

indicators.note: about says the jury's word goes around the single letter

parts.note: a rider is a recommendation a jury adds to its verdict

explanation.surface: A jury's verdict concerning a wartime bomber.
explanation.walkthrough: A rider is an extra recommendation attached to a jury's verdict; 'about' wraps it round A.
explanation.definitionFit: A raider is an attacking aircraft that drops bombs on a target.

clue.text: Conservative 19 shortly put in order

parts.note: the political right is the conservative side
the answer to 19 across, the newspaper boss, is shortened to its common abbreviation ed

explanation.surface: A Tory newspaper chief quickly tidied things up.
explanation.walkthrough: 19 refers to the answer at 19 across, the news boss; 'shortly' takes its abbreviation ED.
explanation.definitionFit: To have righted something is to have set it straight or corrected it.

clue.text: Main race meeting

parts.note: the main is the sea, so this is a gathering for races on the water

explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' looks like 'chief', but it is the old word for the open sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A regatta is a series of boat races, a sporting event on water.

clue.text: Holy man in an unusual role in an inn

definitions.text: Holy man in an unusual role in an inn

indicators.note: in says the saint is placed inside the rearranged letters
unusual signals that the letters of role are reordered

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for saint, a holy man

explanation.surface: A saint finds himself oddly employed at a tavern.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' rearranges ROLE to OLER, and 'in' puts ST (saint) inside. The whole clue paints the answer: a man with a job at an inn.
explanation.definitionFit: An ostler looked after the horses of guests staying at an inn.

clue.text: Punishment for the big and robust

definitions.meaning: a beating with a leather belt

explanation.surface: A whipping awaits the hefty and burly.
explanation.definitionFit: A thrashing with a belt, and also an adjective for a burly, well-built person.

clue.text: Dress the Spanish star

parts.note: to rig out is to dress or kit out
el is the Spanish for the

explanation.surface: Clothe the Spanish celebrity.
explanation.definitionFit: Rigel is the brightest star in the constellation Orion.

clue.text: Musicologist's shady scene

definitions.meaning: Sir George ... compiled the famous dictionary of music, known as ...

explanation.surface: A music scholar's shadowy setting.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir George Grove founded Grove's Dictionary of Music and Musicians.
explanation.definitionFit: The music scholar's surname, and also a small wood or cluster of trees offering shade.

clue.text: Ray's letter from an old woman, say?

indicators.note: say tells us the word for an old woman is spoken, giving a similar sound

parts.note: gammer is an old rustic word for an old woman, the counterpart of gaffer

explanation.surface: A radiographer receives a note from a grandmother.
explanation.walkthrough: Gammer, an old woman, said in a non-rhotic British accent matches the Greek letter that names the gamma ray.
explanation.definitionFit: Gamma is the third Greek letter, giving its name to gamma rays, high-energy radiation.

clue.text: African port, note, in a part of SE Asia

indicators.note: in says the musical note is placed inside the country

parts.note: Laos is a country in South-East Asia
G is a musical note

explanation.surface: A note found in a South-East Asian country about a West African harbour.
explanation.definitionFit: Lagos is Nigeria's largest city and a major seaport.

clue.text: Like a speech out of the time: of Cicero ?

parts.note: ex is the Latin for out of
tempore is Latin for the time, in the form used after ex, the language of Cicero

explanation.surface: A speech straight from the Roman era of Cicero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of Cicero' tells you to put 'out of the time' into Latin, Cicero's language: EX TEMPORE.
explanation.definitionFit: An extempore speech is delivered on the spot, without preparation.

clue.text: Shirley's. endlessly wild : gusto

indicators.note: wild signals that the remaining letters are thrown into disorder
endlessly says the name loses its final letter

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: Shirley is boundlessly passionate with real enthusiasm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' drops the Y of SHIRLEY, and 'wild' rearranges SHIRLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Relish means keen enjoyment or zest.

clue.text: Bird shows ill-humour about a profligate.

indicators.note: about says the word for ill-humour goes around the other pieces

parts.note: a pet is a fit of sulking or bad temper, as in in a pet
a rake is a dissolute, profligate man

explanation.surface: A bird sulks over a wastrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a pet' is an old phrase for a sulk; PET wraps round A and RAKE.
explanation.definitionFit: A parakeet is a small long-tailed parrot.
